basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: What is potable water?
back: Water safe to drink.

base_cards.front: Name a method that removes dissolved salt from seawater.
back: Distillation.

base_cards.front: What is the solid formed by sewage sedimentation called?
back: Sludge.

base_cards.front: Which organisms carry out bioleaching?
back: Bacteria.

base_cards.front: What two substances must be present for iron to rust?
back: Oxygen and water.

base_cards.front: Which metal commonly galvanises iron?
back: Zinc.

base_cards.front: Which two metals form bronze?
back: Copper and tin.

base_cards.front: Which two metals form brass?
back: Copper and zinc.

base_cards.front: What percentage gold is in 18-carat gold?
What catalyst is used in the Haber process?
back: Iron.

base_cards.front: What does NPK stand for?
back: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

base_cards.front: Which polymer type has covalent cross-links and does not melt on heating?
back: Thermosetting.

base_cards.front: Distinguish renewable from finite resources.
back: Renewable resources can be replenished on useful timescales if managed appropriately.
Finite resources are used far faster than they are replaced, so available reserves decline.

base_cards.front: Define sustainable development.
back: Development meeting **current generations’ needs**.
Without compromising **future generations’ ability to meet theirs**.

base_cards.front: Why is potable water not necessarily chemically pure?
back: It is safe because microbes and harmful substances are sufficiently low.
It still contains **dissolved substances**, so it is not only H₂O.

base_cards.front: Give one purpose of filtering water and one purpose of sterilising it.
back: Filtering removes **suspended solid particles**.
Sterilising kills microorganisms.

base_cards.front: Give two sterilisation methods for freshwater supplies.
back: Chlorine and ultraviolet light.

base_cards.front: Why does filtering seawater not usually make it potable?
back: Ordinary filters do not remove the **dissolved salts**.
Desalination, such as distillation or reverse osmosis, is needed to reduce salt levels sufficiently.

base_cards.front: Describe how distillation removes dissolved salts.
back: Water evaporates, leaving dissolved salts behind.
Vapour is cooled and **condensed** into collected water.

base_cards.front: Distinguish sewage-sludge treatment from effluent treatment.
back: Sludge undergoes **anaerobic digestion**.
Effluent undergoes **aerobic biological treatment**.

base_cards.front: Describe bioleaching of copper compounds.
back: Bacteria help produce a **leachate solution**.
The leachate contains dissolved copper compounds for further metal recovery.

base_cards.front: Why can scrap iron recover copper from copper-salt solution?
back: Iron is **more reactive** than copper.
It displaces copper from its compound, producing copper metal.

base_cards.front: Give two reasons recycling copper can be better than extracting more ore.
back: It conserves **finite ore resources**.
It can require less energy and cause less mining damage than fresh extraction.

base_cards.front: Why can painting fail to protect scratched iron?
back: A scratch breaks the **barrier**.
Water and oxygen can then reach the iron and cause rusting.

base_cards.front: Explain why zinc can protect scratched galvanised iron.
back: Zinc is more reactive and **oxidises preferentially**.
It gives **sacrificial protection** while enough connected zinc remains.

base_cards.front: Why does aluminium resist further corrosion after its surface reacts?
back: It forms an adherent **oxide coating**.
The coating acts as a barrier to further reaction of the underlying metal.

base_cards.front: State a use of stainless steel and a property supporting it.
back: Cutlery or kitchen equipment.
It is hard and **corrosion-resistant**.

base_cards.front: State a use of low-carbon steel and a supporting property.
back: Car body panels.
It is comparatively soft and **easily shaped**.

base_cards.front: Give a use of high-carbon steel and its relevant limitation.
back: Cutting tools need its hardness/strength.
It is **brittle**, which can limit uses requiring bending or impact resistance.

base_cards.front: Explain why aluminium alloys suit aircraft structures.
back: They have **low density**, reducing mass.
Suitable alloys combine this with useful strength.

base_cards.front: Name the three main starting materials for soda-lime glass.
back: Sand, sodium carbonate and limestone.

base_cards.front: What two roles make up a composite material?
back: A **matrix/binder** holds the structure together.
A **reinforcement**, such as fibres, supplies useful strength or other properties.

base_cards.front: State a usual source of each Haber-process reactant.
back: Nitrogen from **air**.
Hydrogen from **natural gas**.

base_cards.front: What happens to ammonia and unused gases after the Haber reactor?
back: Ammonia is cooled so it **liquefies and is removed**.
Unreacted nitrogen/hydrogen are **recycled**.

base_cards.front: Why is untreated phosphate rock not an effective direct fertiliser?
back: It is **poorly soluble**.
Nutrients cannot readily dissolve and become available for plant uptake.

base_cards.front: Name the fertiliser products associated with sulfuric and phosphoric acid treatment of phosphate rock.
back: Sulfuric acid: **single superphosphate**, including calcium sulfate and soluble phosphate compounds.
Phosphoric acid: **triple superphosphate**, mainly calcium dihydrogenphosphate.

base_cards.front: Describe phytomining and the form of the recovered material.
back: Plants absorb metal compounds from soil.
Harvest and burn the biomass.
Ash contains **metal compounds**, requiring further processing to obtain metal.

base_cards.front: An empty basin is 24.50 g; after evaporating 50 cm³ water it is 24.65 g. Calculate residue mass and concentration in g dm⁻³.
back: Concentration = 0.15/0.050 = **3.0 g dm⁻³**.

base_cards.front: A 16 g jewellery alloy is 18 carat. Calculate gold mass and explain why alloying is useful.
back: Gold fraction = 18/24 = **0.75**.
Alloying increases hardness/wear resistance compared with soft pure gold.

base_cards.front: Explain why alloys are usually harder than the pure metal.
back: Pure metal has relatively regular layers of similar-sized atoms.
Other elements introduce different sizes and **distort the layers**.
Layers slide less easily.

base_cards.front: Describe manufacturing clay ceramics.
back: Shape **wet clay** into the required form.
Dry as appropriate and heat strongly in a **furnace**.
The resulting hard material can form pottery or bricks, though it is brittle.

base_cards.front: Explain how LDPE and HDPE can both be made from ethene yet have different properties.
back: Different conditions/catalysts produce different chain arrangements.
LDPE’s greater branching prevents close packing.
HDPE packs more closely, giving higher density and greater rigidity.

base_cards.front: Explain why thermosetting polymers do not melt like thermosoftening polymers.
back: Thermosetting chains have **covalent cross-links**.
These prevent chains moving freely on heating.
Thermosoftening chains are separate, so overcoming intermolecular attractions allows movement and melting.

base_cards.front: State the Haber equation and explain the gas ratio.
back: **N₂+3H₂ ⇌2NH₃**.
One nitrogen molecule reacts with three hydrogen molecules.
Feed gases therefore use a **1:3 nitrogen:hydrogen molar ratio**.

base_cards.front: Explain why high pressure favours ammonia in the Haber process.
back: There are **four gas moles** on the reactant side and **two** on the product side.
High pressure favours fewer gas moles.
Equilibrium shifts towards ammonia, increasing its proportion.

base_cards.front: Name the products from nitric acid and phosphate rock, and link one to fertiliser use.
back: Products include **calcium nitrate**.
**Phosphoric acid** is also produced.
Calcium nitrate supplies plant nutrients in a soluble salt; phosphoric acid can support further phosphate-fertiliser manufacture.

base_cards.front: Describe a controlled experiment showing rust needs both oxygen and water.
back: Use comparable clean iron nails, same time and temperature.
One nail has air and water and should rust.
One has dry air with a drying agent, preventing water exposure.
One has boiled water covered with oil, removing/excluding oxygen; little/no rust in the latter two supports both requirements.

base_cards.front: Explain the four major life-cycle stages and why transport matters.
back: Raw-material extraction/processing.
Manufacture and packaging.
Use over the product’s useful lifetime.
Disposal/reuse/recycling, with **transport between stages** adding energy use and emissions.

base_cards.front: Explain why a reusable glass bottle can have lower impact per use despite higher production energy.
back: Manufacture impact is spread over many uses.
Reuse avoids making a new bottle for every use.
Washing and return transport still consume resources/energy.
Actual reuse count, breakage and travel determine whether the overall comparison is favourable.

base_cards.front: Describe the main wastewater treatment sequence.
back: Screen/remove grit.
Sediment to separate **sludge and effluent**.
Digest sludge **anaerobically**.
Treat effluent **aerobically**, with extra chemical treatment if required by contaminants.

additions.front: Why does a positive chloride test not by itself show water is unsafe?
back: It identifies chloride but does not measure whether its concentration exceeds a safe limit.

additions.front: Which treatment removes suspended solids but not dissolved salts?
back: Filtration.

additions.front: Why can sterilised water still require desalination?
back: Killing microbes does not remove dissolved salt.

additions.front: Why must an LCA compare equal functions?
back: Otherwise a lower impact may simply reflect less service or a shorter lifetime rather than a better product.

additions.front: For reusable energy 20 + 0.5n and disposable energy 2n MJ, when does reuse first save energy?
back: From use 14: equality is at n = 13.3, so the first whole number beyond it is 14.

additions.front: Why is an energy break-even point not a complete environmental judgement?
back: Water, pollution, transport, waste and durability may differ too.

additions.front: Why does rust allow continued corrosion of iron?
back: It can flake away, exposing fresh iron to water and oxygen.

additions.front: Why boil water before adding an oil layer in a rusting test?
back: Boiling removes much dissolved oxygen; oil then limits new oxygen entering.

additions.front: How does aluminium’s surface oxide differ from rust?
back: It forms an attached protective layer that limits further attack.

additions.front: What does steel contribute to reinforced concrete?
back: Resistance to tension, complementing concrete’s resistance to compression.

additions.front: Why do composite properties depend on more than the binder?
back: The reinforcement also supplies properties, such as tensile strength, while the matrix holds and protects it.

additions.front: Why does low equilibrium yield per pass not mean all unreacted Haber gases are wasted?
back: Unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled after ammonia is removed.

additions.front: Does phosphate rock supply the potassium in NPK fertiliser?
back: No. It is a phosphorus source; potassium compounds such as potassium chloride are mined separately.

additions.front: Why can a strong material still be unsuitable for an impact-prone object?
back: It may be brittle and fracture rather than deform safely.
